analysis.one_liner: Temporarily lowers the insurance company deductibles in the federal terrorism insurance backstop after large attacks.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2007 with no cosponsors, referred to the Financial Services Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed the federal terrorism insurance program, created after 9/11, so that when an attack causes more than $1 billion in insured losses, each insurance company's deductible — the amount it must pay before the federal government shares the cost — would drop sharply, starting at 5% of the company's prior-year premiums and staying low until a later attack reset it again. The bill was introduced in the House in December 2007, sent to the Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, and never came up for a vote. It had no cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Insurance companies writing property and casualty coverage, especially commercial property insurers. Under the existing Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, after a certified terrorism event each insurer must absorb a deductible (a set share of its own premiums' worth of losses) before the federal government reimburses a large portion of losses. This bill would have cut that deductible to a small percentage of premiums — starting at 5% in 2008 — whenever an attack caused over $1 billion in industry losses, letting insurers keep collecting premiums while paying far less of their own money after a major attack. Policyholders might have benefited indirectly if insurers, facing less risk, kept terrorism coverage more available and cheaper, but the bill contained no requirement of any consumer benefit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill temporarily reduces the deductible each insurer must pay out of pocket before the federal terrorism backstop covers losses, whenever an attack (or a series of attacks in one area) causes more than $1 billion in industry-wide insured losses.

For 2008 the reset deductible would be 5% of an insurer's direct earned premiums from the prior year, rising by half a percentage point each year until another qualifying attack reset it to 5% again — far below the standard deductible otherwise required under the program.

The Secretary of the Treasury could combine losses from multiple smaller attacks in the same geographic area so they count toward the $1 billion threshold, extending the deductible relief to more situations.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The Terrorism Risk Insurance Act works as a federal backstop: once insurers meet their deductibles, the government reimburses a large share of terrorism losses. Reducing the insurers' deductibles means the federal share of any major attack's losses grows, and there is no provision in the bill requiring insurers to lower premiums in return.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have shifted losses from private insurers onto the federal terrorism backstop: by resetting insurers' deductibles to a low percentage of premiums after any event over $1 billion, the federal government (and ultimately taxpayers) would absorb a larger share of losses from major attacks.
The bill attracted no cosponsors and was never debated or amended in committee, so there was no public weighing of its costs — and no mechanism to pass savings on to insurance customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered insurers real protection: after a large attack, they would pay tens of billions less out of pocket, with the federal backstop absorbing the difference. The cost would fall on the federal program — and ultimately taxpayers — with no offsetting reduction in premiums passed to policyholders written into the bill. The narrow rationale (keeping a single devastated insurer solvent after a $1 billion-plus attack) had some merit, but the bill made no effort to protect consumers or recoup the added federal cost, and it attracted no cosponsors. It died in committee without a vote, so its trade-offs were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 17, 2007, in the closing weeks of the first session of the 110th Congress.
No other House member signed on as a cosponsor.

It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, and on March 28, 2008, to its Subcommittee on Capital Markets, Insurance and Government Sponsored Enterprises; no further action was taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No industry gained. Taxpayers were spared the added federal exposure the bill would have created, and the insurance industry kept its place at the table for the broader TRIA reauthorization debates that followed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, by avoiding added federal exposure

for.name: Rep. Gary Ackerman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 17, 2007, and it was referred to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: House committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Barney Frank, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; after referring it to a subcommittee in March 2008, took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no partisan split is visible in the record; it simply died in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have lowered the deductibles insurers must pay before the federal terrorism insurance backstop pays, shifting more of the cost of large attacks to the federal program. It died in committee, so insurers gained nothing.
Had it passed, taxpayers would have stood behind a larger share of terrorism losses through the federal backstop. Because the bill failed, the existing deductible rules stayed in place.
